Instructions to candidates: You are required to answer ANY FIVE questions. ONLY THE FIRST FIVE QUESTIONS ANSWERED WILL BE MARKED. All the questions carry equal marks. Calculators are allowed.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Define the following:

(i) Exports. (2 marks)
(ii) Exchange rate. (2 marks)
(iii) Currency appreciation. (2 marks)
(iv) Terms of trade. (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Exports.** Exports are the goods and services produced in one country and **sold to buyers in other countries**. They bring foreign currency into the country (for example cocoa, timber or bananas sold abroad by Cameroon) and are counted as a credit in the balance of payments.

**(ii) Exchange rate.** The exchange rate is the **price of one currency in terms of another currency**, that is, the number of units of one currency needed to buy one unit of another. For illustration, if 1 US dollar can be bought for 600 FCFA (hypothetical rate), the exchange rate is 600 FCFA per US dollar.

**(iii) Currency appreciation.** This is a **rise in the value of a currency in terms of other currencies** under a floating (market-determined) exchange rate, so that one unit of the currency now buys more foreign currency than before. Exports become dearer for foreigners and imports become cheaper for residents. (It is the opposite of depreciation.)

**(iv) Terms of trade.** The terms of trade show the **relationship between the prices a country receives for its exports and the prices it pays for its imports**. The net barter terms of trade are measured as:

$$
\text{Terms of trade}=\frac{\text{index of export prices}}{\text{index of import prices}}\times 100
$$

For example, if the export price index is 120 and the import price index is 100, the terms of trade are $\frac{120}{100}\times 100=120$: they have improved, because each unit of exports now buys more imports.

questions.enonce_markdown:
The following are examples of tangible and intangible items of the current account:

- Timber
- Insurance
- Aviation
- Banana
- Dividends
- Interest
- Cotton
- Cocoa

Attempt a classification of the above into visible and invisible items. (4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
In the current account of the balance of payments, **visible items** are *tangible goods* that can be seen, counted and recorded at the customs; **invisible items** are *intangible* services and income flows which cannot be seen crossing the border.

| Visible items (tangible goods) | Invisible items (intangible services and income) |
|---|---|
| Timber | Insurance |
| Banana | Aviation (air transport services) |
| Cotton | Dividends |
| Cocoa | Interest |

- **Timber, banana, cotton and cocoa** are physical goods exported or imported and checked at the border: visible trade (the balance of trade).
- **Insurance and aviation** are services sold to foreigners (or bought from them): invisible trade in services.
- **Dividends and interest** are payments of income from foreign investments and loans: invisible items (investment income).

questions.enonce_markdown: State and explain FOUR (4) reasons for trade restriction. (8 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** Trade restriction (protection) means limiting imports by tariffs (import duties), quotas, embargoes or other barriers. Governments do it for the following reasons.

1. **To protect infant industries.** A new local industry (for example a young food-processing or textile firm) has high costs because it is small and inexperienced and cannot compete with big foreign firms. Restrictions on competing imports give it time to grow, to gain experience and to reach economies of scale.
2. **To prevent dumping.** Dumping is the sale of goods abroad at a price below their cost or below the price charged at home. Foreign firms doing this can drive local producers out of business, so the government imposes extra duties to keep competition fair.
3. **To correct a deficit in the balance of payments.** If the value of imports is greater than the value of exports, restricting imports reduces spending on foreign goods and saves foreign exchange, which reduces the deficit.
4. **To protect employment and local jobs.** Cheap imports may force local firms to close and workers to lose their jobs; restricting imports keeps local industries (and the jobs in them) running and encourages people to buy local products.

*Other reasons that could also be given:* to raise revenue for the government (import duties), to protect national security and public health (ban on harmful goods), to avoid over-dependence on a few foreign suppliers, and to diversify the economy.

**Conclusion.** These arguments have some force, but restrictions raise prices for consumers and may provoke retaliation by other countries, so they should be temporary and carefully chosen.
